title: Partitioning
explain: Partitioning is the logical half of sharding: data is grouped into partitions, and a separate mapping decides which nodes hold each partition. The client's partition key decides the logical partition, consistent hashing turns it into a token, and a keyring maps token ranges to replica sets.
model:
Convention here: *partition* = logical unit of data and routing, *shard* = where it lives (many systems use the words interchangeably).

```
partition key --hash (consistent hashing)--> token --keyring--> token range --> replica set
"user42"                                     0x5A..           [100, 500]  -->  {A, B, C}
                                                                              A = primary (token owner)
```

1. The client supplies a **partition key**, deciding the logical partition of a row.
2. The key is hashed with [consistent hashing](#/sd/f/consistent-hashing) to a **token**.
3. A **keyring** assigns token ranges to nodes; the owner of the token is the **primary replica**.
4. Other replicas are chosen by a placement policy, for example across availability zones and racks.

**One token range corresponds to one replica set**, and replication, rebalancing and failure handling work on ranges, not rows.

The partition key is the decision that is hard to change: a low-cardinality key (country) caps parallelism, a skewed key makes hot partitions, and rows read or written together should share a key. Use many more partitions than nodes so rebalancing moves whole partitions ([token rebalancing](#/sd/f/token-rebalancing), [hash bucketing](#/sd/f/hash-bucketing)).

details.q: A chat service sets partitionKey = country with 40 nodes, ~200 countries and 35% of users in one country. Risk?
details.a: Low cardinality plus skew: all rows with the same key hash to the same token, so one partition (one replica set) carries a third of the load and the hash cannot spread it. Use a higher-cardinality key or add a sub-key.

details.q: Walk through how a request finds its primary node.
details.a: The client sends the partition key, which is hashed to a token; the keyring finds the token range containing it; the range maps to a replica set; the first replica, the token owner, is the primary. Nothing in the row names a node, so ranges can move without changing keys.

details.q: A range has replicas A, B, C all in one rack and the rack switch fails. What happens?
details.a: The range becomes unavailable and may lose data if the rack is destroyed. Replica count protects only against independent failures; placement must spread replicas across racks and zones, otherwise three copies behave like one.

details.q: Token space [0,1000) is cut into 10 ranges with replication factor 3 on 5 nodes. How many ranges does each node replicate?
details.a: 10 x 3 = 30 placements spread evenly over 5 nodes, so 6 ranges per node, about 60% of the data.

details.q: Why create far more partitions than nodes, say 256 on 8 nodes?
details.a: Partitions are the unit of movement. With many small ones a new node simply takes some whole partitions, rather than needing to split data. A node can hold many partitions.

details.q: What is the difference between a partition and a node in `[100, 500] -> {A, B, C}`?
details.a: `[100, 500]` is a token range, the stable logical grouping; `{A, B, C}` is the replica set of nodes that physically store it. Placement can change without changing which partition a key belongs to.

prompts.q: Explain the path from a partition key to the primary node.
points: Partition key chosen by the client
Hashed with consistent hashing to a token
Keyring maps the token range to a replica set
Token owner is primary, others by placement policy

prompts.q: Why is the partition key the hardest decision to change, and what makes a good one?
points: Rows and routing depend on it
Rows used together should share a key

prompts.q: Distinguish partitioning from sharding and explain why systems create many partitions per node.
points: Partition: logical grouping; shard: physical location
One token range corresponds to one replica set
Fine granularity gives even balance and room to grow
